title: Cold-Water Coral Reef Dynamics
context:
A. Unlike their tropical counterparts that rely on symbiotic photosynthetic algae, cold-water corals thrive in dark, nutrient-rich bathyal environments typically between 4°C and 12°C. Found at depths ranging from 50 to over 1,000 metres, these azooxanthellate organisms depend entirely on horizontal currents to deliver suspended particulate organic matter and zooplankton. The primary framework-builder in temperate and sub-polar regions is the scleractinian species Lophelia pertusa, which constructs massive biogenic structures known as carbonate mounds or bioherms over geological timescales.

B. The initiation of a cold-water coral reef begins with larval settlement. Free-swimming planulae require an exposed, stable hard substrate to anchor successfully, frequently selecting glacial erratics, exposed bedrock, or discarded mollusc shells. Once attached, the pioneer polyps secrete calcium carbonate to establish the basal plate. Over successive generations, colonies expand radially. As the skeletal framework branches outward, it alters the local hydrodynamic regime, decelerating near-bed water flow and causing mineral and organic particles to settle around the base of the colonies.

C. This hydrodynamic deceleration triggers the secondary growth phase, termed framework aggradation. Interstitial spaces within the coral matrix become filled with fine-grained sediments, a process known as sediment baffling. The trapped silt and clay reinforce the structural integrity of the accumulating mound, preventing skeletal collapse under its own weight. Concurrently, older colonies beneath the living surface perish due to light deprivation and sediment smothering, leaving dense skeletons that lithify into solid limestone. This continuous upward accretion allows the reef framework to elevate into more accelerated water layers.

D. In the mature phase, the reef structure develops distinct micro-morphologies. The summit or reef crest experiences the strongest hydrodynamic forces, which wash away fine sediment and supply rich food patches. However, extreme current speeds can occasionally cause physical fragmentation of fragile branches. Broken fragments slide down the slopes, forming a transitional rubble apron along the flanks. This rubble apron serves a vital role, stabilising peripheral slopes and creating an extensive network of cavities that shelter cryptic invertebrates, including basket stars and squat lobsters.

E. Cold-water coral bioherms display pronounced biological zonation. The living coral framework is dominated by Lophelia pertusa alongside Madrepora oculata, whose white and orange polyps capture passing crustaceans. On the reef flanks, where current velocities diminish, non-framework species such as gorgonian sea fans and glass sponges dominate the landscape, exploiting residual nutrients. Finally, the basal seabed consists of biogenic sediment and coral rubble, an environment favoured by deposit-feeding holothurians and burrowing polychaetes that recycle organic debris.

F. To document and conserve these fragile habitats, marine researchers utilize a tiered suite of monitoring technologies. Acoustic surveys using multibeam bathymetry produce three-dimensional maps of seafloor topography, delineating mound boundaries across vast areas. For fine-scale ecological assessments, remotely operated vehicles (ROVs) equipped with high-definition cameras collect precise video transects and targeted biological specimens. Additionally, benthic landers anchored on the seabed record continuous environmental parameters, measuring localized current vectors, water temperature, and seasonal turbidity.

title: Managing Noise in Open-Plan Offices
context:
A. Open-plan offices are often designed to make teams easier to reorganise and to use floor space efficiently. Yet removing walls also changes how sound travels: conversations, calls and equipment noise can reach people who are not involved. The result is not simply a louder room. Workers may lose concentration when speech is intelligible, even if its volume is modest. For this reason, workplace designers increasingly treat noise control as a sequence of decisions rather than as the installation of one soundproof barrier.

B. The first decision is to identify what people need to do and where. A design team can map quiet tasks, such as checking figures, alongside collaborative activities such as project discussions. It should also record the location and operating hours of printers, kitchens and other persistent sources. Brief observations and staff interviews help distinguish an occasional disturbance from a recurring one. The resulting activity map is useful because a single average noise reading can hide important differences between areas and times of day.

C. The next stage is to consider the room’s layout and its surfaces. A long, unobstructed route between a speaker and a listener allows speech to travel farther than a layout with storage units or partial screens between them. Screens can interrupt this direct path, but their effectiveness depends on their height and position; a low divider may leave a seated listener exposed. Meanwhile, carpets, upholstered furniture and ceiling panels absorb some sound energy. Hard glass and bare concrete tend to reflect it, potentially making a busy room seem more reverberant. Absorption reduces reflections, whereas a screen mainly blocks or redirects a sound path, so the two measures do different jobs.

D. Designers then decide whether to introduce sound masking. This system uses loudspeakers to add a carefully controlled background sound, commonly described as a soft, steady airflow. Its purpose is not to cancel every conversation. Rather, the added sound reduces the contrast between speech and the background, making distant words less intelligible. A technician first measures the existing sound level and then adjusts the masking system across different zones. If the setting is too loud, it can become a distraction itself; if it is too quiet, it may have little effect. Masking is therefore calibrated, not simply switched on at one uniform level.

E. These interventions can be compared by their strengths and limitations. Absorptive materials reduce reflected sound but cannot prevent every direct conversation from reaching a nearby colleague. Screens offer local separation, yet they may obstruct sightlines or make a compact floor feel enclosed. Masking can improve speech privacy across a broader area, but it does not remove the physical source of a noise. The appropriate combination depends on room geometry, the tasks performed and staff preferences. A team that spends much of the day in confidential calls may need a different balance from one that relies on frequent face-to-face discussion.

F. Finally, noise control should be evaluated after the changes are made. Staff can report whether interruptions have become less frequent, while measurements can show whether sound levels vary sharply between work zones. These forms of evidence answer different questions: a lower reading does not automatically mean that speech is less distracting. If complaints persist, the team can identify the relevant area and adjust a screen, a surface treatment or the masking level. Periodic review is also important because team size and work patterns change. Effective design is thus an iterative process: observe, intervene, assess and refine.

title: The Global Journey of the Potato
context:
A. Archaeological evidence indicates that the wild potato was first domesticated around Lake Titicaca, a high-altitude plateau spanning present-day Peru and Bolivia, roughly 8,000 years ago. Early indigenous cultivators selectively bred bitter, toxic tubers into edible varieties resilient enough to withstand harsh Andean frosts. A pivotal technological innovation was chuño, a primitive freeze-dried product created by exposing harvested tubers to freezing nocturnal temperatures and trampling them to expel moisture. Chuño could be preserved in sealed storehouses for over a decade. This dependable nutritional foundation sustained dense highland populations and fueled the imperial expansion of the Inca Empire.

B. Following the Spanish conquest in the 1530s, conquistadors observed the tuber being consumed by miners in Potosí. The potato crossed the Atlantic aboard returning galleons around 1570, initially entering Europe through the port of Seville. However, its broader acceptance was impeded by deep-seated cultural skepticism. Because the plant belonged to the toxic Solanaceae family, peasants viewed it with dread, suspecting it of causing leprosy. Botanical gardens throughout Italy, Spain, and England cultivated the plant primarily as an ornamental curiosity, valuing its delicate violet blossoms rather than subterranean tubers, which theologians condemned as unmentioned in scripture.

C. The widespread transition from novelty to staple crop gained momentum during the eighteenth century, largely orchestrated through state intervention. Facing recurring grain shortages and warfare, European monarchs recognized the tuber’s superior caloric yield. In Prussia, King Frederick the Great issued the Potato Decree of 1756, compelling regional bailiffs to enforce compulsory planting under threat of corporal punishment. Simultaneously in France, agronomist Antoine-Augustin Parmentier dismantled public prejudice through clever publicity, including stationing armed guards around royal potato fields during daylight to induce local citizens to steal the seemingly precious tubers under cover of darkness.

D. In the British Isles, the crop transformed demographics, most dramatically in Ireland, where tenant farmers became utterly dependent on a single cultivar known as the Irish Lumper. By the early nineteenth century, potatoes supplied the primary caloric intake for nearly two-fifths of the population. However, this heavy reliance on an extreme genetic monoculture proved catastrophic. In 1845, a fungal pathogen called Phytophthora infestans arrived via maritime trade routes, unleashing late blight. The resulting Great Famine caused over one million deaths and triggered massive emigration waves, permanently altering Ireland's demographic trajectory.

E. While European societies integrated the crop, maritime trade networks facilitated its migration to the Asian continent. Portuguese merchants introduced the tuber to coastal enclaves in India, whereas the Manila galleons transported it from Mexico across the Pacific to the Philippines. From there, it penetrated southern China during the late Ming dynasty. Chinese farmers discovered that the potato flourished in degraded hill soils where lowland rice faltered. Consequently, the crop opened up marginal mountainous terrain, mitigating regional famines and sustaining explosive demographic growth across interior provinces.

F. By the twentieth century, the potato had become the fourth most important food crop worldwide, trailing only maize, wheat, and rice. To safeguard the plant's future amidst ecological threats, scientists founded the International Potato Center, known as CIP, in Lima in 1971. Researchers there maintain an extensive germplasm bank harboring thousands of native wild accessions. In an era marked by shifting climatic regimes, modern agronomists exploit the potato's rapid maturation cycle and exceptional water-use efficiency, deploying disease-resistant hybrids to secure food supplies across arid zones.

title: Fabrication and Operational Architecture of Epidermal Bio-Patches
context:
A. The emergence of epidermal electronics has transformed wearable health monitoring from bulky accessories into unobtrusive, skin-conformal biosensors. The fabrication pipeline begins with substrate preparation, where selecting an appropriate base material is crucial. Researchers primarily employ polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) or polyurethane due to their biocompatibility and mechanical compliance. This underlying elastomer layer undergoes oxygen plasma treatment to modify its surface energy, thereby enhancing the adhesion of subsequent conductive layers. Once treated, the elastomeric base is spin-coated to achieve a uniform thickness of approximately fifty micrometres, ensuring that the finished patch conforms seamlessly to the dynamic micro-contours of human skin without provoking mechanical irritation or delamination during physical movement.

B. The second phase involves printing conductive tracks and microelectrode arrays onto the prepared substrate. Rather than utilizing rigid metallic films, engineers deposit serpentine gold wiring via micro-contact printing or laser ablation. This distinctive serpentine geometry allows the circuits to withstand significant mechanical tensile strain without micro-fracturing. Following track deposition, an ultra-thin encapsulation layer composed of silicone elastomer is selectively applied to insulate the circuitry. Critical active zones, specifically the working and counter electrodes, remain exposed. These sites are subsequently functionalised with carbon nanotubes to enhance electron transfer kinetics and expand the effective electroactive surface area available for electrochemical detection.

C. Chemical modification of the exposed electrodes constitutes the third critical stage, known as biochemical functionalisation. To monitor targeted metabolic biomarkers such as glucose, lactate, or cortisol, specific bioreceptors must be immobilised. Enzymes such as glucose oxidase are tethered to the nanostructured electrode using a cross-linking agent, commonly glutaraldehyde, which preserves enzymatic stability under fluctuating thermal conditions. Additionally, a selective semi-permeable membrane, typically Nafion, is cast over the enzyme layer. This membrane acts as a molecular sieve, excluding electroactive interferents like ascorbic acid and uric acid, while a hydrophilic coating is introduced to prevent biofouling caused by non-specific protein adsorption.

D. Sweat harvesting and power management represent the subsequent developmental hurdle. Modern bio-patches integrate laser-patterned microfluidic channels fabricated from hydrophobic polymers. By exploiting spontaneous capillary action, these microscopic conduits channel pristine perspiration from dermal pores directly to the sensing reservoir, eliminating the requirement for active mechanical pumps. To supply sustained electrical energy, contemporary prototypes feature miniature zinc-air micro-batteries or stretchable biofuel cells that generate power directly from lactic acid found in human sweat. These autonomous power units maintain a steady operational voltage while significantly reducing the physical weight and footprint of the wearable assembly.

E. The fifth phase involves data acquisition and wireless telemetry. Raw signals generated by the redox reactions at the electrode interface are minute, often in the nanoampere range. Consequently, an onboard potentiostat circuit amplifies these current outputs before an analog-to-digital converter digitises the physiological readings. These processed data streams are routed to a compact microcontroller that interfaces with a Bluetooth Low Energy transceiver. To conserve power, data packets are not transmitted continuously; instead, the device utilizes an adaptive sleep mode, transmitting telemetry bursts at scheduled intervals or whenever an anomalous physiological spike exceeds pre-programmed baseline thresholds.

F. In the final stage, transmitted biometric data are processed through cloud-based analytics platforms. Cloud servers employ supervised machine learning algorithms to filter environmental baseline drift caused by ambient temperature and sensor degradation. The software cross-references multiple physiological variables—such as sweat rate, electrolyte concentrations, and local skin temperature—to generate a multidimensional metabolic profile. When anomalous deviations indicate potential dehydration, metabolic exhaustion, or acute distress, the cloud architecture triggers immediate visual notifications on the user’s mobile application, simultaneously logging encrypted records within clinical electronic health databases for long-term therapeutic evaluation.

title: The Architecture of Medieval Higher Education
context:
A. During the twelfth century, Western Europe witnessed the emergence of the studia generalia, the institutional predecessors to modern universities. Prior to this urban revival, advanced scholarship was primarily confined to secluded monastic cloisters and cathedral schools. As municipal growth accelerated, scholarly communities coalesced in key European centers. To protect itinerant scholars from arbitrary civic courts, monarchs and popes granted protective charters. Emperor Frederick I Barbarossa established an early precedent with the Authentica Habita, granting scholars legal immunity. Subsequent papal bulls confirmed university autonomy and the ius ubique docendi, which entitled graduates to teach across Christendom without undergoing supplementary local examinations.

B. Institutional governance followed two distinct regional archetypes: the student-dominated guild of Bologna and the magisterial guild of Paris. In Bologna, student collectives studying civil and canon law retained ultimate administrative authority. These student nations elected an undergraduate rector, negotiated employment contracts with professors, and imposed financial penalties on lecturers who arrived late or omitted difficult passages. Conversely, the University of Paris functioned as a guild of master teachers. Faculty members governed admissions, set tuition fees, and enforced institutional statutes, while younger students in the elementary arts faculty remained strictly subordinate.

C. Academic progression commenced within the faculty of arts, the compulsory prerequisite for higher learning. The curriculum centered on the Seven Liberal Arts, divided into the introductory trivium (grammar, rhetoric, and logic) and the advanced quadrivium (arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy). Instruction prioritized Aristotelian dialectic, emphasizing formal logical deduction. After three or four years, a candidate completed an oral examination to become a determiner. Defending a thesis during the annual Lenten disputations yielded the baccalaureus artium, certifying fundamental scholarly competence and permitting the holder to deliver supplementary lectures as an apprentice.

D. Baccalaureate holders could enter three postgraduate faculties: medicine, jurisprudence, or theology, the crowning discipline of academic life. Advanced study was exceptionally arduous; theology scholars often spent over a decade analyzing scripture and the Sentences of Peter Lombard. Achieving the rank of magister or doctor culminated in the inceptio, a formal ceremonial investiture. The candidate defended a final disputation before receiving the licentia docendi. Newly admitted masters were invested with the insignia of scholarly authority: an open book, a gold ring, and the doctoral biretta.

E. Daily classroom instruction relied upon two pedagogical methods: the lectio and the disputatio. During the lectio, a master read authoritative texts aloud, dictating explanatory commentaries, termed glosses, for students lacking personal manuscripts. By contrast, the disputatio was an interactive, highly public debate. The presiding master posed a controversial question; a bachelor defended the proposition against aggressive counterarguments from the audience. On the following day, the master concluded with the determinatio, systematically summarizing opposing arguments before delivering his definitive judgment.

F. Academic publishing was accelerated by the pecia system. Supervised by licensed university stationers, approved master manuscripts were divided into separate unbound quires, or peciae. Scribes rented these sections simultaneously, multiplying book output and reducing copy errors. Meanwhile, to shelter impoverished students facing steep urban rents, benefactors endowed residential colleges. Exemplified by Robert de Sorbon’s foundation in Paris, these establishments gradually evolved from simple boarding houses into thriving collegiate environments providing internal academic tutorials.

questions.why: Đoạn E ghi nhận rằng trong buổi Disputatio, cử nhân phải bảo vệ mệnh đề trước các lập luận phản biện gay gắt ('aggressive counterarguments' hoặc 'counterarguments') từ người nghe.
questions.quote: The presiding master posed a controversial question; a bachelor defended the proposition against aggressive counterarguments from the audience.

questions.prompt: Table: Medieval Teaching Methods | Method: Disputatio | Concluding step: The master delivered his final decision through the ____
questions.why: Đoạn E chỉ rõ sang ngày hôm sau, vị thầy sẽ tổng kết và đưa ra phán quyết kết luận mang tên 'determinatio'.
questions.quote: On the following day, the master concluded with the determinatio, systematically summarizing opposing arguments before delivering his definitive judgment.

questions.prompt: Notes: Text Production and Accommodation | Pecia system: Stations split exemplars into ____ so multiple scribes could copy them
questions.why: Đoạn F cho biết các bản thảo chính thức được phân chia thành các tập rời rạc ('unbound quires' hoặc 'peciae') để nhiều thợ chép có thể thuê sao chép cùng lúc.
questions.quote: Supervised by licensed university stationers, approved master manuscripts were divided into separate unbound quires, or peciae.

title: Resource Recovery Pipelines in Island Environments
context:
A. Small Island Developing States (SIDS) confront acute waste vulnerabilities, marked by geographic isolation, restricted land, and high import dependence. Traditional landfilling has rapidly exhausted vacant land, prompting archipelagic governments to establish integrated recovery systems. The cycle begins at municipal sorting sheds, where mixed refuse undergoes preliminary manual separation. Trained sorters extract hazardous items, electronic discards, and bulk contaminants before the remaining mass moves along slow-moving conveyor platforms.

B. Following pre-sorting, materials are segregated into three primary streams: rigid polymers, glass containers, and organic matter. Rigid plastics, mainly polyethylene terephthalate (PET) and high-density polyethylene (HDPE), are classified by color and resin code. Glass bottles are diverted into separate holding bunkers to prevent fragmentation, while wet organic discards are isolated to prevent cross-contamination. On isolated atolls lacking road infrastructure, community eco-chambers act as regional hubs, using solar-powered balance scales to log household contributions before inter-island barge transport.

C. The handling of plastics focuses on optimizing freight efficiency for overseas transport, as islands lack domestic remanufacturing mills. In processing bays, bottles undergo label stripping and mechanical washing. Automated rotary blades then granulate cleaned containers into irregular flakes. These plastic fragments pass through hot-wash basins filled with caustic soda to eliminate residual adhesives. Once dried by centrifugal blowers, flakes are compacted by high-pressure baling presses into dense cubic bundles, ready for reverse logistics aboard commercial vessels.

D. Conversely, glass is predominantly repurposed locally due to its prohibitive export weight. Cleaned bottles enter mechanical hammer-mill pulverizers, which grind containers into fine particles known as glass cullet. This material acts as an effective substitute for dredged marine sediment in civic construction. Island engineers blend this cullet into permeable paving blocks and seawall reinforcement mortars. Local glass conversion substantially reduces coastal lagoon sand-mining, protecting vulnerable shorelines from tidal erosion.

E. Organic discards, comprising nearly half of all island municipal waste, undergo biological transformation to curtail methane emissions. Solid food wastes are blended with carbonaceous coconut husks before entering enclosed rotating drum bioreactors. Inside, thermophilic digestion stabilizes the organic matrix over fourteen days. The processed sludge then migrates to outdoor vermiculture beds populated by native earthworm colonies. These worms convert the compost into nutrient-rich bio-humus, which local farming cooperatives utilize for soil enrichment.

F. Financial sustainability for these recovery schemes hinges on legislative frameworks. A mandatory container deposit framework stimulates consumer return rates by levying a refundable environmental fee during maritime importation. Additionally, extended producer responsibility mandates oblige commercial distributors to subsidize maritime transport for exported plastics. Advanced facilities now affix digital tracking tags onto baled exports, granting customs officials real-time verification of consignment destinations and eliminating illegal maritime dumping.

questions.prompt: Preliminary sorting | Workers manually take out hazardous goods, ____, and large contaminants.
questions.why: Đoạn A nêu rõ những người phân loại loại bỏ 'hazardous items, electronic discards, and bulk contaminants'. Từ đồng nghĩa: 'hazardous goods' = 'hazardous items', 'take out' = 'extract'.
questions.quote: Trained sorters extract hazardous items, electronic discards, and bulk contaminants before the remaining mass moves along slow-moving conveyor platforms.

questions.prompt: Preliminary sorting | Sorted refuse moves along ____ platforms.
questions.why: Đoạn A chỉ ra khối rác còn lại di chuyển dọc theo 'slow-moving conveyor platforms'. Cụm từ cần điền bổ nghĩa cho 'platforms'.
questions.quote: before the remaining mass moves along slow-moving conveyor platforms.

questions.prompt: Plastics categorization | Rigid plastics are classified by resin code and ____.
questions.why: Đoạn B chỉ rõ nhựa cứng được phân loại dựa vào 'color and resin code'.
questions.quote: Rigid plastics, mainly polyethylene terephthalate (PET) and high-density polyethylene (HDPE), are classified by color and resin code.

questions.prompt: Glass storage | Bottles are placed in distinct ____ to prevent them breaking.
questions.why: Đoạn B khẳng định chai thủy tinh được đưa vào 'separate holding bunkers' nhằm tránh vỡ vụn ('prevent fragmentation').
questions.quote: Glass bottles are diverted into separate holding bunkers to prevent fragmentation, while wet organic discards are isolated to prevent cross-contamination.

questions.prompt: Remote atoll collection | Isolated islands rely on ____ as regional collection centers.
questions.why: Đoạn B đề cập trên các đảo san hô hẻo lánh không có đường sá, 'community eco-chambers' đóng vai trò là các trung tâm khu vực ('regional hubs').
questions.quote: On isolated atolls lacking road infrastructure, community eco-chambers act as regional hubs, using solar-powered balance scales to log household contributions before inter-island barge transport.

questions.prompt: Remote atoll collection | Household deposits are measured on ____.
questions.why: Đoạn B ghi nhận việc ghi lại phần đóng góp của các hộ gia đình bằng 'solar-powered balance scales'.
questions.quote: community eco-chambers act as regional hubs, using solar-powered balance scales to log household contributions before inter-island barge transport.

questions.prompt: Plastic processing: Step 1 | Bottles undergo label removal and ____ inside processing bays.
questions.why: Đoạn C liệt kê hai bước xử lý sơ bộ chai nhựa trong vịnh xử lý là 'label stripping' (gỡ nhãn) và 'mechanical washing'.
questions.quote: In processing bays, bottles undergo label stripping and mechanical washing.

questions.prompt: Plastic processing: Step 2 | Units are chopped into pieces by ____.
questions.why: Đoạn C giải thích các lưỡi dao quay tự động ('automated rotary blades') nghiền nhỏ chai nhựa đã làm sạch thành các mảnh nhỏ vỡ vụn ('flakes').
questions.quote: Automated rotary blades then granulate cleaned containers into irregular flakes.

questions.prompt: Plastic processing: Step 3 | Adhesive residues are dissolved in wash basins containing ____.
questions.why: Đoạn C cho biết các mảnh nhựa đi qua các bồn rửa nóng chứa 'caustic soda' để loại bỏ keo dính sót lại ('residual adhesives').
questions.quote: These plastic fragments pass through hot-wash basins filled with caustic soda to eliminate residual adhesives.

questions.prompt: Plastic processing: Step 4 | Plastic pieces are dried using ____.
questions.why: Đoạn C ghi rõ các mảnh nhựa sau khi rửa được làm khô bằng 'centrifugal blowers' (quạt thổi ly tâm).
questions.quote: Once dried by centrifugal blowers, flakes are compacted by high-pressure baling presses into dense cubic bundles, ready for reverse logistics aboard commercial vessels.

questions.prompt: Plastic processing: Step 5 | Dense bundles are formed by ____.
questions.why: Đoạn C chỉ ra rằng các mảnh nhựa được nén thành các kiện khối đặc bởi 'high-pressure baling presses'.
questions.quote: flakes are compacted by high-pressure baling presses into dense cubic bundles, ready for reverse logistics aboard commercial vessels.

questions.prompt: Plastic processing: Step 6 | Bundled plastics are exported via ____ on commercial vessels.
questions.why: Đoạn C nêu rõ các kiện nhựa sẵn sàng cho hoạt động 'reverse logistics' trên các tàu hàng thương mại quay về.
questions.quote: dense cubic bundles, ready for reverse logistics aboard commercial vessels.

questions.prompt: Local glass reprocessing | Glass is pulverized into powder using ____.
questions.why: Đoạn D giải thích chai thủy tinh được đưa vào 'mechanical hammer-mill pulverizers' để nghiền nát thành hạt mịn.
questions.quote: Cleaned bottles enter mechanical hammer-mill pulverizers, which grind containers into fine particles known as glass cullet.

questions.prompt: Local glass reprocessing | Pulverized glass yields a product called ____.
questions.why: Đoạn D nêu tên vật liệu hạt mịn sau khi nghiền thủy tinh là 'glass cullet'.
questions.quote: grind containers into fine particles known as glass cullet.

questions.prompt: Construction usage | The recycled cullet replaces ____ in civic building projects.
questions.why: Đoạn D khẳng định vật liệu này hoạt động như một chất thay thế hữu hiệu cho 'dredged marine sediment' trong ngành xây dựng đô thị.
questions.quote: This material acts as an effective substitute for dredged marine sediment in civic construction.

questions.prompt: Environmental gain | Repurposing glass reduces local ____ in coastal lagoons.
questions.why: Đoạn D chỉ rõ việc chuyển đổi thủy tinh giúp giảm đáng kể hoạt động 'coastal lagoon sand-mining' (khai thác cát đầm phá ven biển).
questions.quote: Local glass conversion substantially reduces coastal lagoon sand-mining, protecting vulnerable shorelines from tidal erosion.

questions.prompt: Organic waste processing: Phase 1 | Food refuse is mixed with ____ to supply carbon.
questions.why: Đoạn E nêu chất thải thực phẩm được trộn cùng vỏ dừa giàu cacbon ('carbonaceous coconut husks').
questions.quote: Solid food wastes are blended with carbonaceous coconut husks before entering enclosed rotating drum bioreactors.

questions.prompt: Organic waste processing: Phase 2 | Initial breakdown occurs within sealed ____.
questions.answer: rotating drum bioreactors | enclosed rotating drum bioreactors
questions.why: Đoạn E nêu rõ hỗn hợp đi vào 'enclosed rotating drum bioreactors' (thùng phản ứng sinh học quay khép kín) để ổn định trong 14 ngày.
questions.quote: Solid food wastes are blended with carbonaceous coconut husks before entering enclosed rotating drum bioreactors.

questions.prompt: Organic waste processing: Phase 3 | Vermiculture beds house ____ to convert the compost.
questions.why: Đoạn E cho thấy bùn thải chuyển sang các luống nuôi trùn chứa các đàn giun bản địa ('native earthworm colonies') để tạo mùn hữu cơ.
questions.quote: The processed sludge then migrates to outdoor vermiculture beds populated by native earthworm colonies.

questions.prompt: Policy & oversight | Outbound plastic bales are tracked using ____ to prevent illicit dumping.
questions.why: Đoạn F khẳng định các cơ sở gắn 'digital tracking tags' lên các kiện hàng xuất khẩu để hải quan giám sát và ngăn chặn xả thải trái phép.
questions.quote: Advanced facilities now affix digital tracking tags onto baled exports, granting customs officials real-time verification of consignment destinations and eliminating illegal maritime dumping.
